title: Transport Information Beyond Strong Eigenstate Thermalization
authors: Avadhut V. Purohit, Harshit Sharma, Udaysinh T. Bhosale
abstract: Strong eigenstate thermalization (ETH) in operationally mean-ergodic, non-chaotic systems provides an opportunity to investigate whether Floquet eigenstates retain information about classical transport beyond their leading thermodynamic behavior. We address this question using the double kicked top (DKT), which exhibits nonmixing transport and dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport under variation of its control parameters. We show that the coefficient $m$ of the leading finite-size correction to the normalized eigenstate entanglement entropy (EE) $s$ tracks the restructuring between these transport regimes even when the thermodynamic-limit entropy $c$ becomes nearly insensitive to them. This coefficient $m$ is positive for nonmixing transport and negative when dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport dominate. The coefficient's sign reversal in the coexistence regime remains stable as the semiclassical resolution increases. Our results demonstrate that finite-size eigenstate structure can encode signatures of classical transport that are invisible in the thermodynamic-limit entropy, providing an eigenstate-based diagnostic of dynamical organization beyond the leading thermodynamic behavior associated with strong ETH.
summary: This paper uses the Double Kicked Top model to probe how quantum eigenstates encode information about classical transport regimes beyond standard thermalization predictions. By analyzing the finite-size correction to the entanglement entropy, the authors define a coefficient that robustly tracks the transition between nonmixing and weak mixing dynamics. This demonstrates that quantum structure can reveal subtle details about classical dynamics otherwise hidden in the bulk thermodynamic limit.
main_problem: The study investigates whether quantum eigenstates retain information about underlying classical transport mechanisms (e.g., nonmixing vs. weak mixing) beyond the leading thermodynamic predictions of Strong Eigenstate Thermalization (ETH).
main_result: The finite-size structure, quantified by the Structure Refinement Coefficient (SRC), successfully tracks the transition between different classical transport regimes, revealing signatures invisible in the thermodynamic-limit entropy.
method: The analysis uses finite-size scaling of the bipartite entanglement entropy (EE) to extract the SRC, which is then correlated with the long-time decay of classical correlation functions.
model_or_system: The research employs the Double Kicked Top (DKT) model, a system whose dynamics can be tuned to exhibit regimes ranging from operationally mean-ergodic nonmixing transport to dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport.
key_observables: Normalized Entanglement Entropy (EE), Structure Refinement Coefficient (SRC, $m$), and long-time classical correlation amplitudes ($\langle C_{O,\infty} angle_{	ext{ens}}$).
important_parameters: Control parameters $k_r$ and $k_	heta$, which tune the system between nonmixing, weak mixing, and coexistence transport regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the leading finite-size correction to the normalized EE follows a linear scaling form, $s(N) = c + m\epsilon(N) + O(\epsilon(N)^2)$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the persistence of classical correlations in different regimes (nonmixing vs. weak mixing) and show the SRC ($m$) exhibiting a stable sign reversal as the system parameters cross a critical point.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the diagnostic tools by analyzing classical correlations in the DKT. It then applies these tools to the quantum entanglement entropy, showing that the SRC coefficient $m$ serves as a sensitive probe of the underlying classical dynamics, even when the thermodynamic entropy $c$ saturates.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, quantifiable diagnostic tool—the SRC—to distinguish between different types of dynamical organization (e.g., integrable vs. chaotic) in quantum systems, going beyond simple thermalization measures.
